rows.description: A teenager recognises thumbs-down and rude gestures, including the raised middle finger, as insults or strong disapproval, and learns to step back, stay calm and tell an adult if it comes from bullying. Using them hurts others and can bring consequences.
A young adult reads the thumbs-up, folded-hands and wave emoji as modern equivalents of gestures, but the thumbs-up may seem curt or passive-aggressive to some. Norms differ by age and workplace.

rows.subtype: My view is the only view [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler hides his face and believes no one can see him, or shows a picture facing himself. He cannot yet imagine that others see differently.
An older child begins to understand that friends may believe or want different things, but still struggles when his own strong feelings are involved.
A teenager feels that his experiences are unique, that nobody has felt this before, and that everyone is watching him. It gradually softens as he meets more people.
Adults worry when a quiet child prefers being alone and push them into groups. Checking for real distress is wise, but preference for solitude is often just temperament.
A friend notices someone slowly declining every invitation and replying less. Gentle, low-pressure reaching out matters, since withdrawal often grows quietly when nobody checks.
A young man tells his family clearly that he will not take dowry and that the marriage will not depend on it. Speaking early, with firm respect, protects both the bride and his own integrity.
A relative who objects to dowry or gender pressure says so calmly at the planning stage and finds allies among elders. Change is often slower than anger, but one clear voice makes others braver.
A teenager checks hair, fixes clothes or hides behind a phone when feeling watched. It can signal self-consciousness, ordinary grooming or a wish to look good; teasing about it deepens insecurity.

rows.subtype: Covering the mouth and cultural norms [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young adult covers the mouth when laughing, yawning or coughing, which shows manners in many places but shyness in others. It can also signal surprise or embarrassment, so meaning depends on the cultural setting.

A young adult picks up a phone, taps or scrolls in awkward moments as a comfort or an escape. It may show boredom, anxiety or urgent work, and others often read it as disrespect; a short explanation prevents hurt.
A child hears repeatedly the story of how they were born, how the family struggled or what a grandfather did. Family narratives give a child a place and a sense of belonging.
A young adult labelled as the difficult one or the lazy one in the family lives inside that story. Stepping out of an assigned role takes many small acts of behaving differently.
